summary: Rossella and Deepsha from Sprout Social deliver a talk on moving from AI experimentation to becoming truly AI-first, acknowledging they are in the messy middle of their transformation with no finished playbook. They define AI-first as a mindset shift: moving from sprinkling AI into existing features to reimagining what new experiences are possible, with AI at the center of strategy. Unlike previous shifts (cloud, mobile, DevOps) that disrupted one area at a time, AI disrupts product, architecture, people, process, and ethics simultaneously. Being AI-first is not binary but a multi-dimensional evolution. They introduce a framework with three dimensions: Strategy (what you prioritize and why), Ways of Working (how you build, ship, and adapt), and People (how teams evolve and the skills that define success). On Strategy, the key shift is from asking where to add intelligence to existing experiences to asking what entirely new experiences AI makes possible. This creates an innovator's dilemma: shipping current customer needs while investing in a fast-moving future. Roadmaps become less deterministic, embracing ambiguity where learning and discovery shape the path. They illustrate with a hypothetical puppy health app (Wufill) showing how an AI-first unified experience transcends individual feature teams. On Ways of Working, they advocate ritualized discovery (repeatable, deliberate experimentation built into planning cycles), MVPs for learning rather than just launching, treating process as a product evaluated against outcomes, and smart velocity—speed paired with direction. On People, they emphasize that AI transformation is fundamentally cultural, requiring T-shaped talent (deep expertise plus wide versatility), and pathfinders who can navigate ambiguity and imagine paths that don't yet exist. They stress that becoming AI-first isn't just about AI specialists—it requires building fluency across the entire organization through newsletters, cross-functional show-and-tells, and a self-service platform enabling product and engineering teams to prototype AI features without deep AI team involvement. Yet some fundamentals remain unchanged: AI features must still solve real customer problems rooted in needs rather than novelty, and UX, performance, reliability, and trust remain non-negotiable. Human creativity, judgment, and care stay central to leadership and decision-making. They close with advice for leaders: get honest about trade-offs, invest in people not just models, kill the roadmap if needed, be bold, learn out loud, and ship unconventional ideas. They frame the talk as a flashlight in the maze, noting the journey won't be linear or perfect, and frame AI not merely as a technological revolution but a human one.

sections.title: Introduction & Defining AI-First
sections.summary: Rossella and Deepsha introduce themselves and frame the talk as a candid real-time look at Sprout Social's AI transformation. They define AI-first as a mindset shift from sprinkling AI into features to rethinking planning, building, and value delivery through an AI lens. They contrast AI with prior tech shifts that disrupted one area at a time, noting AI disrupts everything simultaneously.

sections.title: Three-Dimension Framework
sections.summary: They introduce a simple framework for navigating AI transformation across three dimensions: Strategy (what you prioritize and why), Ways of Working (how you build, ship, and adapt), and People (how teams evolve and skills that define success).

sections.title: Strategy: From AI-Enhanced to AI-First
sections.summary: The strategic shift moves from asking where to add intelligence to existing experiences to asking what new experiences are possible. This creates an amplified innovator's dilemma requiring enterprise discipline and startup curiosity in parallel. Roadmaps shift from deterministic to ambiguity-driven. The Wufill puppy app example illustrates how AI-first unifies value across feature silos into a seamless experience.

sections.title: Ways of Working: Ritualized Discovery & Smart Velocity
sections.summary: They advocate for ritualized discovery as a repeatable, deliberate process; MVPs for learning where failure is a feature; treating process as a product evaluated against outcomes; and smart velocity—speed paired with direction. Old linear processes designed for predictable roadmaps no longer hold up, but too many new processes create drag.

sections.title: People: Cultural Transformation & T-Shaped Talent
sections.summary: AI transformation is fundamentally cultural. They identify two shifts: how talent evolves and how to scale AI fluency. They advocate for T-shaped talent combining deep specialization with wide versatility, comparing it to Indiana Jones—combining the scholar and the adventurer. Pathfinders who can navigate ambiguity and imagine paths that don't yet exist are essential.

sections.title: Org-Wide AI Fluency & Self-Service Platform
sections.summary: Becoming AI-first requires building fluency across the whole organization, not just among AI specialists. Everyone touches AI—marketers, designers, PMs, care agents. They invest in org-wide AI fluency through newsletters, podcasts, cross-functional show-and-tells, and empowering teams to use AI tools. They aim to build a self-service platform enabling product and engineering teams to prototype and ship AI features without deep AI team involvement, making AI thinking the default rather than the exception.

sections.title: What Hasn't Changed & Closing Reflections
sections.summary: Some fundamentals remain unchanged: AI features must still solve real customer problems rooted in needs, not novelty. UX, performance, reliability, and trust stay non-negotiable. Human creativity, judgment, and care remain central to leadership. They advise leaders to get honest about trade-offs, invest in people, kill the roadmap if needed, be bold, learn out loud, and ship unconventional ideas. They close framing the talk as a flashlight in the maze—AI transformation won't be linear or perfect, but you only need the right questions and conviction to start. They frame AI as a human revolution, not just a technological one, requiring time, grit, and patience.

demonstrations: Wufill puppy health app example showing unified AI experience across meal tracking, activity, digestive insights, and supplement recommendations versus narrow feature-by-feature responses
limitations: No finished playbook exists—this is a candid reflection from the middle of the journey, not from the finish line
AI transformation looks different for every company
Introducing too many new processes all at once can backfire and create drag
The journey is not linear and will include setbacks, doubts, and growing pains
quantitativeClaims: A three-month roadmap starts to feel stale in three weeks
AI makes the innovator's dilemma 10 times harder
